entities.summary:
Guinness World Records, originally published as The Guinness Book of Records in 1955, has emerged as a cultural touchstone in global history, documenting both extraordinary human feats and the extremes of nature. The inception of this reference book can be traced back to Sir Hugh Beaver, who sought to resolve pub arguments regarding record-setting achievements. Co-founders Norris and Ross McWhirter played a pivotal role in its establishment in London, ensuring that the publication would not only entertain but also serve as an authoritative source on the remarkable and bizarre aspects of life around the globe.

The first edition was launched in 1955 and quickly became a bestseller, with its unique blend of trivia and record-breaking achievements capturing the public's imagination. The publication has undergone numerous updates, with editions now spanning across various languages and formats. By 1999, the title had evolved to include a broader spectrum of records, reflecting changing societal interests and the emergence of new categories such as technology, sports, and environmental milestones. Notably, the Guinness World Records Day, celebrated annually, encourages record attempts worldwide, further solidifying its role in popular culture.

The legacy of Guinness World Records extends beyond mere entertainment; it has influenced the way we perceive achievements and challenges in society. The book has inspired a sense of competition and ambition, with countless individuals striving to break records, thereby creating a global community of record-setters. Educational institutions often utilize the records for teaching purposes, highlighting the intersection of knowledge, curiosity, and achievement.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Guinness World Records (originally published as The Guinness Book of Records) is an annual reference book published by Guinness World Records Ltd., first published on 27 August 1955 by the Guinness Brewery as a commercial gift for pub landlords. The first edition was compiled by twin brothers Norris (1925–2004) and Ross McWhirter (1925–1975) after managing director Sir Hugh Beaver was unable to settle a pub argument about whether the golden plover or the grouse was Europe's fastest game bird — the concept was that a book of verified facts about superlatives (the fastest, the tallest, the oldest, the heaviest, the most numerous) could settle similar disputes and serve as a promotional tool for the brewery.

The Guinness Book of Records became one of the bestselling copyright books of all time — it has appeared on The New York Times bestseller list more than any other book, has sold over 143 million copies in more than 100 countries, and has been published in at least 37 languages. Its annual publication (first as a UK edition, expanded globally from the 1960s) made it a fixture of Christmas gift-giving in the English-speaking world — 'looking up records in the Guinness Book' became a cultural ritual that persisted for decades, and the book's role as a family reference and object of wonder established it as one of the most widely owned reference books in history.

Guinness World Records transformed the concept of the 'record' from a competitive sporting achievement into a cultural category — the pursuit of Guinness records became a global participatory phenomenon, generating thousands of record-breaking attempts annually in categories from athletics to eating, from the bizarre to the inspiring.
